query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Optimal Al content drives the formation of a fine, coherent ordered γ′ phase within the FCC matrix, which reinforces the alloy by impeding dislocation motion and acting as a barrier to radiation‐induced defects.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high‐entropy alloy exhibiting a nominal single‐phase FCC structure.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the Al content by ±5–10 at.% relative to the equiatomic composition while holding other elemental ratios constant.
generation.conditions: Subject the alloys to isothermal heat treatments around 800 °C in an inert atmosphere to promote ordering without oxidation, followed by radiation exposure and cryogenic mechanical testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The size, distribution, and coherence of the γ′ precipitates within the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: An optimal increase in Al content (within a limited window of approximately 5–10 at.% variation) promotes local chemical ordering that forms a fine, coherent γ′ phase. This phase not only retards grain coarsening and strengthens the alloy through precipitation hardening but also serves as barriers to defect migration and recombination of radiation‐induced defects, thereby enhancing radiation tolerance alongside high‐temperature strength and cryogenic toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline equiatomic alloy, the optimized alloy will display a stable dual-phase (γ + γ′) microstructure with improved tensile strength at high temperatures, lower oxidation rates, heightened radiation damage resistance, and superior crack‐blunting behavior at cryogenic temperatures.
generation.baseline: Standard equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy with a single-phase FCC structure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is effective only within a restrictive Al concentration window; excessive Al can form brittle intermetallic phases, while too little Al fails to induce sufficient γ′ precipitation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in mechanical, oxidation, and radiation properties and the optimal Al concentration window (estimated near a 5–10 at.% deviation) require further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant correlation is observed between variations in Al content, the emergence and characteristics of a γ′ phase, and the improvements in oxidation resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness, the hypothesis is falsified.

The low yield strength of FCC-structured HEAs, which is typically just 200 MPa in the as-cast form, is a significant disadvantage, as it is significantly less than the necessary strength of metallic structural materials [,]. To overcome these limitations in mechanical properties, a proposed method is to manufacture an HEA composed of a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix with an ordered FCC structure (L12) precipitated phase, i.e., the γ′ phase, by adding Al + Ti. An HEA based on a γ + γ′ alloy system exhibited excellent thermal stability, coarsening resistance, and strength retention around a temperature of 800 °C [,,,]. The γ′ phase is an ordered phase with an almost exact stoichiometric composition ((Ni, Co)3(Ti, Al)) in the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA, with γ′ depending on the Al + Ti content []. Alloys used in extreme environments, such as turbines and aero-engines, require excellent high-temperature strength and oxidation resistance. Recent progress in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which have five or more elements present in near-equimolar proportions, has resulted in several alloys with excellent high-temperature strength. However, the oxidation and corrosion behavior of HEAs is still poorly understood and modeled. Oxidation is an extremely complex process where kinetics, thermodynamics, and microstructure play a competing role in forming the passivating oxide layer, which prevents a catastrophic oxidation [,]. Challenges in modeling the oxidation behavior of HEAs are numerous, including understanding the role of chemistry, microstructure, grain boundaries, associated volume changes, stresses in the oxide scale, and the environment itself, along with the thermodynamic stabilities at elevated temperature and the kinetics of the process. We attempt a piecewise approach toward modeling the oxidation behavior of HEAs and to address a critical question in this work—how do the composition and the microstructure affect the oxidation behavior of the HEAs?
